extracted.intended_audience: researchers applying for ERC Starting, Consolidator, Advanced, or Synergy grants (prospective PI applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for preparing successful ERC grant applications (B1/B2, CV/track record, and interview) across Starting, Consolidator, Advanced, and Synergy calls. Emphasizes proposal content, PI independence, and stage-specific expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground-Breaking Is Non-Negotiable
rubrics_metrics.description: ERC's defining criterion: the proposal must articulate paradigm-shift potential — 'This will change how we think about X'. Incremental work is explicitly disfavored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame research as capable of changing the field; explicitly state the novel, paradigm-shifting contribution. Avoid framing the work as incremental improvements. Use language and objectives that make the transformative potential clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-Risk / High-Gain Framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers look for high-risk, high-gain projects. The project should be ambitious and risky but promise substantial payoff if successful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine a bold vision with concrete feasibility evidence and explicit risk mitigation. State contingency outputs: 'If this works, transformative; if not, still produces X, Y, Z.' Demonstrate that risk has been considered and mitigated rather than ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single PI Excellence and Independence
rubrics_metrics.description: ERC funds a single PI as the intellectual driver; the PI must be shown as the sole intellectual leader with an independent track record. Dependence on senior mentors ('senior PI parasitism') is a known killer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the PI's independent contributions explicit (especially relative to previous supervisors). Emphasize solo intellectual leadership, unique ideas, and an independent research trajectory. Limit the role of collaborators when they could be perceived as replacing PI independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: B1 Synopsis Is Crucial
rubrics_metrics.description: The 5-page B1 is read by all panelists and decides Step 1 evaluation; it must work as a standalone document and functions like NIH Specific Aims but longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure B1 clearly and concisely conveys the central question, why it's ground-breaking, the high-level methodology, feasibility evidence, and impact. Because many applicants are filtered at Step 1, invest disproportionate effort in making B1 self-contained and compelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 Strategy (B1 + CV + Track Record)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1 is scored from the B1, CV, and track record only; approximately ~30% of applicants progress to Step 2. Panel reads, scores, and ranks based on these materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design materials so B1 and CV together form a coherent case for excellence and transformative potential. Remember: a strong CV can rescue a weaker B1; a weak CV cannot be rescued by a strong B1. Make sure the B1 can be evaluated independently of B2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2 Strategy (B2, External Review, Interview)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2 includes the full proposal (B2), external reviews by field experts, panel synthesis, and often an interview for shortlisted candidates (8–15 minute presentation + Q&A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a detailed B2 that expands and substantiates B1 claims, anticipate specialist scrutiny, and prepare concise, persuasive interview slides and answers. Expect external reviewers in your exact subfield and tailor B2 to convince specialists while remaining coherent for the panel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track Record Selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Select ~10 publications with explanations that make your major contributions and independence clear. Provide a narrative of major contributions and independent work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each selected paper, include a short rationale describing your specific intellectual contribution. Highlight leadership roles (first-/senior-author, PI-led projects), invited talks, and other signs of independent achievement to separate you from mentors.

rubrics_metrics.name: CV Conventions and Career Narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: The CV should present a career narrative that evidences independence: mobility (institutions/countries), fellowships/awards, plenary talks/keynotes, editorial roles, leadership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the CV to show progression towards independence (e.g., PI-led grants, supervision, unique line of research). Include indicators of esteem (awards, keynote/plenary talks, editorial positions) and demonstrate international mobility if applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: B1 Section a) State of the Art and Objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: 1–2 pages situating the field: describe where the field is, what's missing, present your bold question, and list specific objectives (3–5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concise mapping of the current state, explicit gaps, and a clearly formulated bold research question. Use 3–5 specific, linked objectives that directly address the gap and feed into a single transformative aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: B1 Section b) Methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: 2–3 pages on how you'll address each objective: why chosen methods, risks and mitigations, feasibility evidence, and timeline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each objective, explain the methods, justify their appropriateness, present preliminary data or feasibility indicators, identify key risks, and propose concrete mitigation strategies. Include a realistic timeline to show deliverability.

rubrics_metrics.name: B1 Section c) Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 page describing scientific impact (paradigm shift) and broader societal/economic impact. For ERC, scientific transformative impact is primary; broader impacts are secondary but mention career trajectory benefits for applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize scientific/disciplinary impact: explain how results would change thinking or open new fields. Mention societal/economic impact succinctly and, for Starting/Consolidator applicants, state how the grant will advance the PI's career trajectory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Starting Grant: expectations and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: For applicants ~2–7 years post-PhD: narrative must demonstrate junior independence; scope should be ambitious but feasible for an early career PI. Typical budget ~1.5M EUR over 5 years (approx.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize early independence, clear rationale for chosen scope, and how the project establishes a distinct research direction. Use selected publications and roles to show emerging leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidator Grant: expectations and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: For applicants ~7–12 years post-PhD: applicants should have an established lab and be consolidating a research direction. Typical budget ~2M EUR over 5 years (approx.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate leadership of a group and a coherent, ambitious direction that builds upon prior independent work. Show evidence of sustained productivity and group management skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advanced Grant: expectations and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: For very senior applicants (10+ years post-PhD) with established international standing: propose visionary, transformative projects. Typical budget ~2.5M EUR over 5 years (approx.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize international leadership, a major new direction or capability, and a track record of high-impact outputs. The project should be bold and field-changing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synergy Grant: multi-PI justification and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: For groups of 2–4 PIs whose complementary expertise is required to address a problem; justify why multiple PIs are necessary. Typical budget ~10M EUR over 6 years (approx.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly specify each PI's distinct contribution and intellectual leadership. Justify why the problem cannot be tackled by a single PI and how the synergy produces transformative outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Winning Themes (aggregate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common factors among successful proposals: 1) Bold vision that could change the field; 2) Strong CV with independent track record; 3) Methodology with credible feasibility; 4) Risk mitigation built in; 5) Single-PI intellectual coherence; 6) Genuine cross-disciplinary novelty; 7) Clear independence from previous mentors; 8) Strong host institution commitment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist as a final alignment test: does the proposal present a bold, coherent vision led by a demonstrably independent PI with plausible methods and institutional support? Make sure cross-disciplinarity is substantively integrated, not superficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Losing Themes (aggregate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common reasons for rejection include: incremental project framing; methodology too vague; track record showing dependence on senior collaborators; scope too narrow for ERC ambition; risk without mitigation; generic or unsupported 'impact' claims; mismatch between project ambition and the grant level applied for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid these pitfalls by clearly articulating novelty and scope, providing methodological detail and feasibility evidence, demonstrating independence in the CV, including explicit risk mitigation, and tailoring ambition to the grant category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand ERC vs NIH Cultural Differences
rubrics_metrics.description: ERC values single-PI vision, long-term transformative work, cross-disciplinary boundary-pushing, European mobility narrative, and risk-taking. NIH tends to value team science, clinical/translational impact, established methodology, productivity per dollar, and conservative risk-mitigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If transitioning from an NIH-style mindset, reframe proposals to emphasize a single PI's visionary research and higher tolerance for risk. Avoid over-emphasizing team-based or strictly translational justifications that are more NIH-aligned unless they genuinely serve the ERC vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview Format and Preparation (Step 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviews (when held) typically involve an 8–15 minute presentation followed by Q&A with a panel and sometimes external experts. Slides in English are expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a concise, narrative-driven presentation that clearly states the vision, methods, and risk mitigation. Practice direct answers to likely criticisms, anticipate specialist questions, and allocate time for clear, confident delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successful Interview Behaviors
rubrics_metrics.description: What wins interviews: clear, confident articulation of vision; direct answers to questions; acknowledging weaknesses with mitigation; engagement with feedback; energy and conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be concise and honest when addressing weaknesses; show how mitigations make the plan feasible. Avoid reading slides, and demonstrate command of the proposed science and its transformative potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview Pitfalls (What Loses Interviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: Behaviors that undermine interviews: reading slides, defensive posture, ignoring panel concerns, giving vague answers, and lacking conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice to avoid reading slides; respond to panel concerns directly; prepare crisp, evidence-backed answers; maintain composure and conviction even when challenged.
